rows.grounds: having the nature of one's own self

items.question: Why does one who sees all realities as one's own self perceive no sameness among them?
premises: Realities are truly real in their own nature
They appear as forms of one's own self
Seeing them as self-nature removes imposed uniformity
items.inference: For one who perceives realities as forms of the self, there is no mere sameness among them.
items.plain_english: For one who sees realities as true forms of one's own self, there is no sameness among them.

items.question: Must tranquility be imagined at the beginning of an action?
premises: Action has a beginning
Tranquility may be posited conceptually
The question concerns whether such positing is required
items.inference: Tranquility is considered something to be imagined at the beginning of action.
uncertainties: The force of vā atha as presenting an alternative or addition is context-dependent
items.plain_english: Or else, tranquility is to be imagined at the beginning of an action.

rows.grounds: in the first daily section or chapter

items.question: Where has the matter under discussion already been definitively established?
premises: A prior determination exists
The first daily section is the locus of that determination
The matter is treated as settled
items.inference: This has indeed been ascertained in the first daily section.
items.plain_english: This has indeed been ascertained in the first daily section.

rows.grounds: in the intermediate space or gap

items.question: Does any isolated state of pure quiescence exist in the interval between actions?
premises: An interval between moments is considered
A state could be imagined as existing there
The verse denies such an isolated state
items.inference: There is no such state existing alone in the interval here.
uncertainties: The vocative-like force of yāhi in this context is interpretive
items.plain_english: And there is no such state existing alone in the interval here.

items.question: What arises in place of a supposed isolated gap between conscious acts?
premises: No isolated quiescent state persists in the interval
Desire or will continues to unfold
Another desire of the same kind arises
items.inference: Another desire of the same kind indeed spreads forth again.
items.plain_english: Indeed, another desire of the same kind spreads forth again.

items.question: How can desire fail to arise where establishment in self-experience is absent?
premises: Self-experience may be unestablished
Desire arises in relation to such lack of establishment
The verse challenges the absence of desire in that condition
items.inference: Where there is no establishment in self-experience, how could desire not arise?
items.plain_english: Where there is no establishment in the experience of the self, how could desire not arise?

rows.grounds: of a stone and similar things
in the state of being inert

items.question: How can Śiva-nature be established even in the insentience of a stone?
premises: Stones and similar things are considered insentient
The doctrine asserts Śiva-nature pervades all
An apparent contradiction is raised
items.inference: The verse questions how Śiva-nature is established even in the insentience of stone and the like.
items.plain_english: How, in your view, is Śiva-nature established even in the insentience of a stone and the like?

items.question: What follows immediately after an action has become fruitful and completed?
premises: An action can be fruitful
An action can reach completion
The moment immediately after completion is considered
items.inference: The discussion turns to what occurs immediately after a fruitful and completed action.
items.plain_english: Immediately after an action has become fruitful and completed.

items.question: Why do the powers of Śiva remain established without interruption after action?
premises: The powers of Śiva exist
These powers are eternally abiding
Their abiding explains continuity beyond completed action
items.inference: Because the powers of Śiva exist and are eternally established, no true gap occurs.
items.plain_english: Because the powers of Śiva exist, and those powers are eternally established.

rows.grounds: of the free and autonomous one

items.question: By whom could the will of the independent Lord be externally determined or imagined?
premises: The Lord is independent
Will belongs to the Lord
External determination would contradict independence
items.inference: No one can imagine or determine the will of the independent Lord.
items.plain_english: By whom could the will of the independent Lord be imagined?

rows.grounds: of statements declaring the universe insignificant
of those who speak for the sake of dispassion and such aims
rows.morph: compound: vairāgya+dispassion + ādi+and-others + artha+purpose + vādinām+speakers, m.gen.pl

items.question: What is the intended purpose of statements declaring the insignificance of the universe?
premises: Some statements declare the universe insignificant
Such statements are spoken for specific aims
Dispassion and related aims motivate those speakers
items.inference: Statements about the universe's insignificance serve the purpose of cultivating dispassion and similar aims.
items.plain_english: Regarding statements about the insignificance of the universe, spoken for the sake of dispassion and the like.

items.question: How does differentiation down to the atomic level appear within a single body?
premises: A single body is considered
Differentiation is observed within it
This differentiation extends down to atoms
items.inference: Even in one body, differentiation extends down to the level of atoms.
items.plain_english: But in one single body, because of differentiation reaching down to the atom.

items.question: Why is no fault found in multiplicity when grounded in a single substratum?
premises: Multiplicity may be traced to one substratum
An objection might be raised against such multiplicity
The single substratum removes the objection
items.inference: Even for them, there is no fault when grounded in one substratum.
items.plain_english: Or even from a single substratum, there is no fault in them either.

rows.grounds: by the expansion of Śiva whose nature is one consciousness
rows.morph: compound: eka+one + cit+consciousness + svarūpa+nature + śiva+Śiva + prasaraṇena+by-expansion, n.inst.sg

items.question: How does the expansion of Śiva as one consciousness account for apparent multiplicity?
premises: Śiva's nature is one consciousness
Expansion of that nature is posited
This expansion can account for what appears
items.inference: Apparent multiplicity can be understood through the expansion of Śiva, whose nature is one consciousness.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse
items.plain_english: Or to that extent, by the expansion of Śiva whose nature is one consciousness.

items.question: Why must all things be understood as the abiding presence of Śiva?
premises: A mistaken way of knowing is rejected
The expansion of one consciousness has been indicated
Śiva abides as all
items.inference: Therefore, all is to be understood as Śiva abiding.
items.plain_english: Here it should not be understood otherwise; therefore, Śiva abides as all.

rows.grounds: by the removal of all objections

items.question: How does the preceding reasoning remove all objections against Śiva's all-pervading nature?
premises: Objections regarding multiplicity and insentience were raised
The doctrine of one consciousness expanding as Śiva was presented
This reasoning addresses those objections
items.inference: Thus, by the removal of all faults, the position is secured.
items.plain_english: Thus, by the removal of all objections.

items.question: What textual division is marked at this point in the work?
premises: The text is organized into daily sections
A concluding marker is given
This marker identifies the section number
items.inference: This marks the end of the third daily section.
items.plain_english: The third daily section.

items.question: Can any reality be truly incapable if all things participate in Śiva's power?
premises: Capability and incapability are being examined
The existence of any truly incapable thing is questioned
The doctrine implies universal participation in power
items.inference: No one is found to be incapable, nor is any thing merely capable in a limited sense as you suppose.
uncertainties: The exact contrast intended by te api no is compressed and interpretive
items.plain_english: No one is found to be incapable, and in your view no thing is merely capable either.

items.question: Does a greater power bind or constrain a lesser power as an external force?
premises: Differences in degree of power are observed
One power may be greater than another
The relation between greater and lesser power is questioned
items.inference: If one has greater power, it may appear to bind one with lesser power.
items.plain_english: Now, if one has greater power, it binds the one with lesser power.

items.question: If the capable one can act, does that imply a separate capability in another?
premises: A capable agent can accomplish action
Capability might be attributed to another
The verse denies an independent other capability
items.inference: If it is said that the capable one can act, this does not establish a separate capability in another.
items.plain_english: If it is said that the capable one is able to act, then there is no separate capability in another.

items.question: Do individual objects like pots possess their own independent capability?
premises: Objects such as pots appear individually
Capability might be attributed to each separately
Independence would follow from separate capability
items.inference: The verse raises the view that individual capability in things like pots would amount to independence.
uncertainties: Whether this states a position to be accepted or refuted depends on the following verse
items.plain_english: The capability of pots and the like, taken individually, would be independence.

items.question: Who alone is the truly capable and independent agent manifesting in various ways?
premises: Independent capability cannot belong separately to many objects
Only one ultimate agent can be truly capable
Śiva manifests in various ways
items.inference: Only Śiva alone abides as the capable one, manifesting thus in various ways.
items.plain_english: One alone abides as the capable one, Śiva indeed, manifesting in various ways.

rows.grounds: having the form of the infinite universe

items.question: Why must the principle of consciousness be one while appearing as the infinite universe?
premises: Multiple independent capable agents are not possible
Śiva alone is the capable reality
Consciousness appears as the infinite universe
items.inference: Therefore, the principle of consciousness is one alone, having the form of the infinite universe.
items.plain_english: Therefore, it cannot be otherwise: the principle of consciousness is one alone, having the form of the infinite universe.

items.question: Why is true being identical with the supreme truth and therefore with Śiva?
premises: What truly exists is real
Ultimate reality is the highest truth
That highest truth is identified as Śiva
items.inference: What is real is the supreme truth, and that supreme truth is Śiva.
items.plain_english: What is real is indeed the supreme truth, and that supreme truth is therefore Śiva.
